subject: Lumina Health — inference config: H100/A100/L4 tradeoffs & fallbacks

Subject: Initial capacity questions for Dedicated (H100/A100/L4)

Hi Priya,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — the latency numbers looked promising. Procurement asked me to get a clearer recommendation for the Dedicated capacity we should reserve if we sign a 12-month commitment. Our workload is a mix of:
- Clinical note summarization and long-context QA (average context 40k tokens, some up to 120k)
- Short-chat assistant for patients and staff (mostly <512 tokens)
- Embeddings for nightly batch indexing

High level questions:
1) For this mix, should we prioritize H100s (memory/long-context) or A100s (balanced) vs L4s (cost-effective short context)?
2) Can we safely hedge with a small L4 pool for bursty low-latency traffic without risking model quality regression?
3) Any guidance on cushion sizing (headroom %) for production SLOs?

We plan to share usage curves once procurement approves a sizing call. Can you include an estimate for monthly committed vCPU/GPU hours and an example fallthrough policy?

I attached our draft MA plan. Looking forward to a short call next week.

Best,
Natalie

Lumina Health

Subject: Re: Initial capacity questions for Dedicated (H100/A100/L4)

Hi Natalie — thanks for the clear summary and the MA draft. Short answers up front, then a proposed plan we can refine on the call:

Quick guidance (tl;dr):
- For heavy long-context (40k-120k): H100-dense pool is strongly recommended for predictable latency and KV-cache residency.
- For steady medium-context and embedding compute: A100s are a cost-effective middle ground and handle mixed batches well.
- For bursty low-latency short requests (<512 tokens): L4s are a cheap and reliable fallback if you accept a tiny step-down in model capability for simple assistant flows.
- Cushion: recommend 20–30% headroom for QPS peaks; increase to 40% if you expect frequent unexpected load (e.g., release-day patient onboarding).

Proposal (we'll walk through numbers on the call):
1) Baseline pool split (initial commit): H100 50% / A100 35% / L4 15% — rationale below.
2) Hedging: auto-burst policy to move some short-chat QPS to L4 during non-critical windows, with automatic rollback to A100/H100 when latency or QoE deviates by configured thresholds.
3) Memory vs perf: pin longest-context jobs to H100 exclusively; use A100 for mixed workloads with quantization Q4_0 where possible; reserve L4 for stateless short interactions and non-critical batch embedding builder jobs.

We'll include a worked example for your MA (monthly committed GPU hours, expected token throughput, and per-token estimate) plus a fallthrough policy draft.

Looping Dev and Aditya for technical sizing details — Dev, can you sketch assumptions for context-window memory footprints and expected effective throughput per GPU for Lumina's workload? Aditya / Jordan — can you prepare a short ops note on how we'd implement the fallthrough policy and billing guardrails?

Thanks,
Priya
Priya Natarajan
Senior Solutions Lead, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial capacity questions for Dedicated (H100/A100/L4)

Natalie / team — adding the engineering assumptions so procurement has numbers to work with. These are conservative estimates based on Redwood benchmarks and Lumina's described mix.

Assumptions:
- Long-context runner: model variant with 70k average context, quantized to Q2_K; effective resident KV footprint per request ~32 GB. H100 with 80GB memory per card is required to avoid sharding across too many devices for sub-500ms token latency for streaming workloads.
- A100 (40GB) supports batches of mixed mid-length requests (<=16k context) at ~0.6x the H100 per-card throughput for large-context but is cheaper per-hour.
- L4 (24GB) is optimized for short contexts; we see ~3–4x tokens/sec for tiny requests vs H100 when used with smaller context windows and fp16 quantization, but quality for long-context summarization degrades significantly.

Throughput guidance (approx, tokens/sec per GPU under typical configs):
- H100 (long-context tuned, medium batch): 130 tokens/sec effective for 32k contexts (streaming).
- A100 (mixed workloads): 220 tokens/sec for short/medium mixes (because smaller KV overhead), but for heavy long-context it drops to ~80 tokens/sec.
- L4 (short context): 600 tokens/sec for <512 token dialogs.

Example commitment calc (monthly):
- If you expect 1M long-context tokens/day -> roughly 1.5 GPU-days/month on H100 (rough back-of-envelope, we will produce an exact calc).
- Embedding nightly batch (200M vectors/day) likely better on A100 fleet for throughput and cost.

Operational notes:
- KV caching is critical: pin frequent patient-history prefixes to H100 cluster cache to reduce per-request recompute.
- Tiered autoscaling: keep a hot H100 pool at min capacity for latency SLO, warm A100 pool for scaling bursty mixed traffic, and L4 as low-cost overflow.

I'll prepare a short table with exact GPU-hour estimates for your MA. Will share by tomorrow.

—Dev
Dev Patel
Principal Inference Engineer, Redwood Inference

Natalie — quick note on how fallthrough and billing guardrails would work in Redwood Dedicated: 

Implementation sketch:
- Route policy: requests labeled by route (patient-assistant-chat, long-note-summarize, nightly-embed) -> routing table that maps to pools.
- Fallback triggers: CPU/GPU queue depth > threshold OR end-to-end latency above SLO OR explicit per-request quality score drop.
- Fallback actions (in order): 1) reroute to warm A100 pool; 2) if still constrained, route to L4 for short-context flows only (with transparent header returned to client to allow graceful degradation messaging).
- Billing guardrails: fallthrough usage counts against burst credits, and if burst credits are exhausted, we throttle non-critical traffic (e.g., nightly embed batch) rather than degrade clinical workflows.

Suggested default thresholds for Lumina pilot:
- H100 min hot pool: 4 cards (reserve for streaming long-context SLO)
- A100 warm pool: scale from 6 -> 18 cards based on 15-min rolling QPS
- L4 overflow: up to 8 cards for short-chat bursts

I'll prepare an ops-runbook snippet and the YAML for the routing table you can drop into your infra as an example.

—Aditya
Aditya Rao
Head of Solutions Architecture, Redwood Inference
